content: Targeted prevention programs should be implemented for young sex workers and other key populations. For adolescents at high risk of acquiring HIV, these programs should include the provision of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). Evidence from research and programmatic experience highlights the importance of combining information dissemination, counseling, provision of commodities, and health services with structural interventions. These structural actions include legal and policy support to improve access to sexual and reproductive health services and community mobilization to address social and gender norms. In terms of treatment and care, early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in people living with HIV has been shown to achieve viral suppression, which reduces both the rates of sexual transmission of HIV and the occurrence of clinical events. Additionally, HIV self-testing and community-based testing and treatment approaches have the potential to increase HIV diagnosis rates, facilitate the initiation of ART, and improve viral suppression outcomes. Mental health interventions should be integrated into HIV care services for all individuals living with HIV, with a particular focus on adolescents. Linkages to mental health services should be established in settings where healthcare infrastructure and trained personnel are available. However, significant attention is needed to address gaps in prevention strategies, their implementation, and access to high-quality services. In 2016, only 64 out of 107 UNAIDS reporting countries had a strategy or plan related to adolescents and HIV. Most adolescents lack basic knowledge about HIV prevention. Between 2012 and 2017, only 34% of young men and 28% of young women in sub-Saharan Africa had comprehensive knowledge of HIV prevention. Adolescent girls, in particular, may face challenges in negotiating condom use due to factors such as economic dependence, interpersonal violence, and power imbalances related to age and gender. From 2011 to 2016, condom use during the last high-risk sexual encounter in the previous 12 months was reported to be less than 50% among young women aged 15–24 years in 31 countries and among young men aged 15–24 years in 18 countries. Female-controlled prevention options, such as PrEP, offer an additional choice for young women at risk. Adolescents are less likely than adults to undergo HIV testing. In nearly 60% of the 107 reporting countries, parental consent was required for adolescents to access HIV treatment. Innovations like HIV self-testing, where adolescents can perform the test privately, provide an opportunity to expand services. However, it is crucial to include counseling and referral information within self-test kits to address adolescents' questions and help them cope with test results. Adolescents living with HIV are underserved by existing HIV services. They experience poorer retention in care and lower rates of viral suppression compared to children and adults living with HIV. States have obligations under human rights law to provide HIV prevention and care to adolescents. This includes ensuring access to confidential HIV testing and counseling services, as well as evidence-based prevention and treatment programs delivered by trained personnel who respect adolescents' rights to privacy and non-discrimination. States must also ensure that the right to health for children, including adolescents, is not compromised by discrimination, including that based on HIV status. Removing barriers such as third-party consent requirements is part of states' obligations to ensure access to HIV prevention, testing, and treatment as components of sexual and reproductive health services. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued specific guidance for adolescents regarding HIV testing, counseling, treatment, and care. Recommendations include community-based approaches to improve treatment adherence and retention in care for adolescents living with HIV. Health facilities should provide HIV testing and counseling services with linkages to prevention, treatment, and care for adolescents in all epidemic settings. Adolescents should be counseled on the potential benefits and risks of disclosing their HIV status and supported in deciding whether, when, how, and to whom to disclose. WHO guidelines also emphasize the importance of initiating ART in all adolescents living with HIV, regardless of clinical stage or CD4 cell count. First-line ART regimens for adolescents should include two nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors plus either a non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitor or an integrase strand transfer inhibitor. For older children and adolescents with more therapeutic options, third-line ART regimens may include novel medicines used in adults, such as etravirine, darunavir, and raltegravir. In settings with high prevalence of malaria or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be continued into adulthood. In low-prevalence settings, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis may be discontinued for clinically stable or virally suppressed children aged 5 years and older who have been on ART for at least six months and have a CD4 count above 350 cells/mm³. Adolescent-friendly health services should train healthcare workers to support treatment adherence and improve retention in care for adolescents living with HIV. Counseling should empower adolescents to make informed decisions about disclosing their HIV status. States must ensure that adolescents' rights to health, privacy, and non-discrimination are upheld, and barriers to accessing HIV services, such as third-party consent requirements, are removed.
